scenes.title: How do you build a line that can never meet this one?
scenes.narration: Suppose you are given y equals two x plus five, and you need a different line through three comma negative four that is parallel to it. Here’s the idea: parallel lines do not stay apart by accident. They have the same rate of change, so they move in exactly the same direction.

scenes.title: Parallel means SAME slope
body: Different intercept keeps the lines distinct
scenes.narration: For nonvertical lines, parallel means equal slopes. A slope of two means every time x increases by one, y increases by two. If two lines make that same change forever, their vertical separation stays constant. This is where students often mix things up: opposite slopes are not parallel; keeping the same slope is the key.

scenes.title: Use the new point to find the new intercept
scenes.narration: Now keep the slope two, but do not copy the old intercept five. The new point determines where the new parallel line sits. Substitute x equals three and y equals negative four into y equals two x plus b. That gives negative four equals six plus b.

scenes.title: Solve for the vertical shift
scenes.narration: Subtract six from both sides, so b equals negative ten. The new equation is y equals two x minus ten. Notice why the intercept changes: the slope controls direction, while the intercept controls vertical position. Same slope plus a different intercept gives a distinct parallel line.

scenes.title: Check BOTH conditions
scenes.narration: Quick check: plug in x equals three. Two times three minus ten equals negative four, so the line passes through the required point. Its slope is still two, matching the original line, so the lines are parallel. Recap the idea: parallel lines share a rate of change, and the new point fixes the new intercept.
